_comment: Points of interest. Properties: name, kind (capital | cult | city | fortress | imperial | ruins | village), start/end BCE years of existence, mode (both | biblical | archaeological), popup {bible, archaeology, source}. Coordinates approximate, after Pleiades/AWMC.

popup.bible: The City of David, capital of the United Monarchy, then of Judah alone. The Temple of Solomon stood here from c. 960 BCE until Nebuchadnezzar burned it in 586.
popup.archaeology: In the 10th century BCE a highland town of a few thousand people, no monumental buildings; the 'great kingdom' of the Bible is not in the ground. By the 8th century it is a real city — Hezekiah's Broad Wall and the Siloam Tunnel date from then.

popup.bible: Capital of the northern kingdom, built by Omri (1 Kgs 16:24). Condemned by the prophets as the seat of idolatry; destroyed by Assyria in 722 BCE.
popup.archaeology: A major 9th-century building project with an acropolis and a massive casemate wall — the archaeology of a real state. Assyrian records call the north the 'House of Omri.' After 722 it became an Assyrian provincial capital.

popup.bible: Guarded the Jezreel Valley pass on the Via Maris. The place Josiah died in 609 BCE trying to stop Pharaoh Necho (2 Kgs 23:29). In Christian tradition, the site of Armageddon ('har Megiddo').
popup.archaeology: A heavily fortified Canaanite city-state in the 10th century — not part of Solomon's empire. Its famous 'Solomonic' gates date to the 9th-century Omride dynasty. Destroyed around 609, matching Josiah's death.

popup.bible: Second city of Judah, besieged by Sennacherib in 701 BCE while his envoy demanded Jerusalem's surrender (2 Kgs 18-19).
popup.archaeology: The Assyrian siege ramp is still visible, with hundreds of arrowheads and the famous 'Lachish reliefs' from Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh. The Lachish letters — ostraca from 588 BCE — record the last days of the kingdom, city by city.

popup.bible: Northernmost shrine of the northern kingdom, where Jeroboam set up a golden calf (1 Kgs 12:29) — the rival altar the Judahite scribes condemned.
popup.archaeology: A huge sacred precinct with a monumental podium, a 'bamah,' and a cultic installation with bulls — not an idol, but a pedestal for Yahweh. The Tel Dan Stele (c. 840 BCE) — 'House of David' — was found in the city's gate.
popup.source: Tel Dan excavations; Tel Dan Stele

popup.bible: Where Jacob dreamed of a ladder to heaven (Gen 28). Jeroboam set up the southern golden calf here (1 Kgs 12:29).
popup.archaeology: A major highland sanctuary from the Iron Age; the 'golden calf' archaeology is debated, but the site's cultic importance is clear. Destroyed in the 8th century.

popup.bible: A Judahite fortress in the Negev; the Bible barely mentions it.
popup.archaeology: The only Judahite temple ever excavated, with two incense altars in the Holy of Holies — one with frankincense residue, one with cannabis mixed with dung. Deliberately dismantled, probably by the Josianic reform.

popup.bible: Where the exiles were carried in 597, 586, and 582 BCE. Ezekiel's visions happen by the Chebar canal here. The Psalms of lament are Babylonian poetry.
popup.archaeology: The imperial capital of the Neo-Babylonian empire; Nebuchadnezzar's palace ration tablets list 'Jehoiachin, king of Judah.' The Cyrus Cylinder (539 BCE) records the Persian policy of return.
popup.source: Babylon excavations; Jehoiachin ration tablets; Cyrus Cylinder

popup.bible: The 'city of blood' of the prophet Nahum; Jonah's reluctant destination. Its fall in 612 BCE is the hinge that freed Josiah.
popup.archaeology: Capital of the Assyrian empire; Sennacherib's palace walls carried the reliefs of the Lachish siege. Sacked by Babylonians and Medes in 612 BCE.

popup.bible: Capital of Aram, Israel's recurring northern enemy; the Arameans 'oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz' (2 Kgs 13:22).
popup.archaeology: Head of the Aram-Damascus kingdom; in 853 BCE its king Ben-Hadad led the coalition that stopped Assyria at Qarqar. Destroyed by Tiglath-Pileser III in 732.

popup.bible: Phoenician city that supplied Hiram's cedar and craftsmen for Solomon's temple (1 Kgs 5); Jezebel's homeland.
popup.archaeology: A wealthy maritime city-state on an island; its purple dye and trade network spanned the Mediterranean. Never conquered by Assyria — only by Babylon after a 13-year siege.

popup.bible: 'The head of all those kingdoms' (Josh 11:10); burned by Joshua in the conquest narrative.
popup.archaeology: The largest tell in Israel, 200 acres; its 10th-century 'Solomonic gate' is now dated to the 9th century (Omride). Destroyed by Assyria in 732 BCE.

popup.bible: Given to Solomon by Pharaoh as a dowry (1 Kgs 9:16) and rebuilt by him.
popup.archaeology: A Canaanite city-state that stayed independent through the 10th century; its six-chambered gate is 9th-century, not Solomonic. The Gezer Calendar (10th c. BCE) is one of the oldest Hebrew texts.

popup.bible: Covenant site of Abraham and Joshua; first capital of the northern kingdom under Jeroboam I (1 Kgs 12:25).
popup.archaeology: A major highland city with the earliest Israelite-period fortifications; the 'Shechem' of the Amarna letters was already prominent in the 14th century.

popup.bible: Moabite city taken by Israel, according to the Bible; where the Mesha Stele's king ruled.
popup.archaeology: Found in 1868 at Dibon: the Mesha Stele, c. 840 BCE, records Moab's rebellion against Israel after Omri's death — and names the god Chemosh dragging Yahweh's vessels before him.

popup.bible: Capital of Ammon; besieged and taken by David (2 Sam 12:26-31).
popup.archaeology: Ammon's hilltop capital (modern Amman) with its citadel; Ammonite inscriptions confirm the kingdom's wealth and its own divine council under the god Milcom.

popup.bible: Capital of Edom; the prophets thunder against it (Amos 1:12).
popup.archaeology: A walled Edomite town with a casemate wall and a rich archive of seals and ostraca; Edom's rise dates to the 8th-7th centuries, powered by the Arabian trade.

popup.bible: Solomon's Red Sea port, where his fleet sailed for Ophir's gold (1 Kgs 9:26-28).
popup.archaeology: The gulf port (near modern Aqaba/Eilat) is real — a gateway for the Arabia trade; the Bible's 'ships of Tarshish' aside, archaeology confirms the port's existence.

popup.bible: Not in the Bible — and that is the point.
popup.archaeology: A 9th-century way-station in the Sinai desert with wall inscriptions and painted figures reading 'Yahweh of Samaria and his Asherah' — the goddess beside the god, on the road between the kingdoms.

popup.bible: Never mentioned in the Bible.
popup.archaeology: Site of the 853 BCE battle where Shalmaneser III met an anti-Assyrian coalition. The Kurkh Monolith lists Ahab of Israel with 2,000 chariots — the largest chariot force in the alliance.

popup.bible: Unnamed in the Bible, but the hinge of the exile.
popup.archaeology: In 605 BCE Nebuchadnezzar crushed Egypt's army here, ending Egyptian power in the Levant and making Babylon the superpower that would destroy Jerusalem in 586.

popup.bible: The Egyptian capital of the oppression narratives; 'the pride of Egypt' the prophets threaten (Jer 46:19).
popup.archaeology: Egypt's ancient administrative capital; the pharaohs who marched through the Levant — from Ramesses III to Necho II — passed through here.

popup.bible: One of the five Philistine capitals; where the ark was taken after its capture (1 Sam 5).
popup.archaeology: The largest Iron Age olive-oil production center known — 115 olive presses — making it the industrial powerhouse of the Philistine coast.

popup.bible: Goliath's city (1 Sam 17); where David pretended madness (1 Sam 21:10-15).
popup.archaeology: Tell es-Safi — at 50+ hectares, the largest Philistine city, destroyed by Hazael of Damascus around 830 BCE, exactly when the biblical text says Gath was taken (2 Kgs 12:17).

popup.bible: Not in the Bible — but the deep south where Yahweh's name first appears.
popup.archaeology: The copper-mining center of the Arabah. An Egyptian temple here (14th-12th c.) was reused by Midianites, whose smelting camps name the local god in inscriptions — the metallurgical world where some scholars place Yahweh's origins.

popup.bible: Pre-biblical — the name 'Yahweh' in a text that predates Israel.
popup.archaeology: Egyptian topographical lists (13th c. BCE) name the 'Shasu of Yhw' — semi-nomadic pastoralists roaming Seir, Edom, and Teman. The earliest external witness to the god's name, before Israel existed.
popup.source: Egyptian inscriptions at Amarah West & Soleb

popup.bible: Where the ark rested in the tabernacle; Samuel's sanctuary (1 Sam 1-4).
popup.archaeology: An Iron Age I shrine site destroyed around 1050 BCE — matching the ark's capture narrative. One of the few places where archaeology and the biblical timeline of the pre-monarchic period agree.

popup.bible: Not in the Bible; the Medes' summer capital (Ezra 6:2 says the scroll of Cyrus was found 'in the citadel of Ecbatana').
popup.archaeology: Capital of the Median kingdom, the empire that helped topple Nineveh in 612 and Babylon in 539 — the east that Cyrus inherited.

popup.bible: The south anchor of the land — 'from Dan to Beersheba.' Abraham's well (Gen 21).
popup.archaeology: A well-planned fortified city with an underground water system; the horned altar found dismantled here echoes the reform that centralized worship in Jerusalem.

popup.bible: The walls that fell at the trumpet blast (Josh 6).
popup.archaeology: The walls that did not fall: the famous Bronze Age walls collapsed centuries before Joshua, and the city was nearly unoccupied when the Bible says it was conquered. The conquest narrative is theology, not reportage.

popup.bible: Where the sun stood still (Josh 10); where Saul's descendants were executed (2 Sam 21).
popup.archaeology: A major highland city with a 25-meter water shaft — engineering of a real, organized polity in the Iron Age.

popup.bible: Philistine city where the ark was taken (1 Sam 5); Amos thunders against it (Amos 1:8).
popup.archaeology: A major Philistine port and cultural center; its excavation revealed the material culture of the 'Sea Peoples' who settled the coast.

popup.bible: Philistine seaport; Samson's birthplace (Judg 14).
popup.archaeology: One of the great Bronze-to-Iron Age ports; a 12th-century BCE infant burial site here revealed Philistine origins in the Aegean world.

popup.bible: Where Samson pulled down the temple on the Philistine lords (Judg 16); the southern gateway of the Via Maris.
popup.archaeology: The hinge of the coastal route between Egypt and the Levant — every army from Thutmose III to Alexander marched through it.

popup.bible: Abraham's burial place (Gen 23); David's first capital (2 Sam 2).
popup.archaeology: A highland town with an impressive Iron Age wall; the 'patriarchal' period archaeology remains famously silent.

popup.bible: The setting of Esther; where Nehemiah served the Persian court (Neh 1:1).
popup.archaeology: The winter capital of the Persian empire, whose kings — Cyrus and his heirs — ruled the returning exiles' world.

popup.bible: The 'tribes' settling the promised land.
popup.archaeology: The signature of early Israel: hundreds of small, unwalled, terraced hillside villages with pillared houses and storage silos — a population boom of indigenous highlanders, not foreign conquerors.

popup.bible: 'How lonely sits the city that was full of people!' (Lam 1:1). The temple a memory, the king in chains.
popup.archaeology: Destruction layers, Babylonian arrowheads, and a devastated city — the ground confirms the text for once. The Babylonian exile was real, and it changed everything.

popup.bible: Where Gedaliah governed what remained of Judah after 586 (2 Kgs 25:22-25).
popup.archaeology: Tell en-Nasbeh, 12 km north of Jerusalem: the administrative center of the Babylonian province of Yehud — proof that some Judahites stayed and kept the land.

popup.bible: Not in the Bible — the diaspora was bigger than the return.
popup.archaeology: A Jewish garrison on the Nile with its own temple to YHW, documents written in Aramaic — proof that Yahwism thrived in Egypt long after the exile, and that its goddess Anat was still worshipped there.

popup.bible: First capital of the northern kingdom before Omri built Samaria (1 Kgs 15-16).
popup.archaeology: Tell el-Far'ah (North), a well-planned city with a palace complex; its early Iron Age sequence is the clearest archaeology of the northern kingdom's first decades.

popup.bible: Where Israel camped 38 years and Miriam died (Num 20); the gateway of the exodus route.
popup.archaeology: A Judahite fortress in the desert; the exodus itself left no trace — the 13th-century 'wilderness wandering' has no archaeological footprint.

popup.bible: Not in the Bible — but the exiles' own city.
popup.archaeology: A Babylonian town whose archive of cuneiform tablets (c. 572-477 BCE) names hundreds of exiles: 'Yahudu' — 'Judah.' The names show Yahwistic identity rising in the next generation, not dissolving.
